questions.question: Will WTI Crude Oil (WTI) hit (HIGH) $100 in October?
questions.resolution_criteria:
This market will resolve to "Yes" if, at any point after market creation and during a trading session of October 2026, any Pyth 1-minute candle for the Active Month of ICE Futures Europe WTI Crude Futures (denoted by Pyth as "CLL") has a final "High" or "Low" price equal to or beyond (above for ↑ High Prices, below for ↓ Low Prices) the listed price. Otherwise, this market will resolve to "No".

Prices will be used exactly as published by Pyth, without rounding.

Only prices achieved during an applicable trading session of the specified timeframe's business days will be considered (See: "Trading Hours" at https://www.ice.com/products/213/WTI-Crude-Futures). The trading session for a given business day typically begins at 8:00 PM ET on the prior calendar date, except for the session dated Monday, which begins at 6:00 PM ET on the preceding Sunday, and where modified by holiday or other special hours (See: https://www.ice.com/holiday-hours).

The Active Month is the nearest listed contract, except during that contract's final three trading sessions. At the open of the third-to-last trading session, the next listed contract becomes the Active Month.

Each contract's last trading day will be determined by ICE Futures Europe per the WTI Crude Futures contract specification (generally the 4th US business day prior to the 25th calendar day of the month preceding the contract month, or five US business days prior if the 25th calendar day is not a US business day). The last trading day for each contract is posted at https://www.ice.com/products/213/WTI-Crude-Futures/expiry.

For example, if the last trading session for the nearest listed contract is the session for Monday the 20th, the next listed contract would become the Active Month at the start of the trading session for Thursday the 16th (8:00 PM ET on Wednesday), assuming a standard trading calendar.

If the relevant Pyth data is unavailable due to a system outage, data failure, or other disruption that prevents verification of the required 1-minute candle data, the official daily high/low price published for the Active Month WTI Crude Oil Futures contract by ICE Futures Europe may be used to determine whether the listed price was reached during the applicable trading session (See: https://www.ice.com/report/10 with "T-West Texas Intermediate Light Sweet Crude Future" selected).

In the event of a contract specification change, feed change, or similar structural modification affecting the underlying market during the listed time frame, this market will resolve based on adjusted prices as displayed on Pyth.

If the Active Month contract does not trade at all during the listed time frame, this market will resolve to "No".

The resolution source for this market is Pyth — specifically, the ICE Futures Europe WTI Crude Futures Active Month "High" and "Low" prices available at https://app.pyth.com/explore?search=CLL, with the chart settings configured for 1-minute candles. Historical 1-minute candles may be accessed by appending a Unix timestamp (seconds) to the Pyth chart URL using the "t=" parameter.

forecasts.rationale: The June ceasefire collapsed in July and the US has kept a blockade of Iranian ports since July 14. CENTCOM's last confirmed strikes on Iranian territory in the sources found were Aug 30 and Sept 1. On Oct 8 Trump said the US will not attack Iran before the Nov 3 midterms while the blockade stays, and CBS (Oct 11) reported no recent US strikes on Iranian land. Enforcement at sea (a ship disabled in the Gulf of Oman Oct 10) does not count, but Houthi attacks on Riyadh, the weekend Hormuz mine incidents and stalled talks leave real escalation risk through Oct 31.

Base rate for escalation during a prolonged pause in similar conflicts is moderate (~30-40% chance of strike in a 3-week window), but the evidence strongly shifts probability toward continuation. President Trump's explicit October 8 statement that the U.S. will not attack Iran before the November 3 midterms while the blockade continues is a clear political commitment backed by a 6-week pause in strikes on Iranian territory (last confirmed Sept 1). The ongoing blockade strategy and lack of recent strikes (per CBS Oct 11) suggest a deliberate choice of pressure over kinetic action. Only a major Iranian provocation or significant Houthi escalation directly attributed to Iran would likely override this electoral calculus before October 31.

The base rate of a direct US strike on Iranian territory in any given month is low, historically around 5%. However, the ongoing U.S.-Israeli war on Iran, the blockade since July, and recent strikes in August‑September raise the risk above the base rate. President Trump’s Oct 8 statement that the U.S. will not attack Iran before the Nov 3 midterms, combined with CBS reports of no recent strikes as of Oct 11, reduces the likelihood of a qualifying action before Oct 31. Taking these factors together yields an estimated ~78% chance that the ceasefire (no qualifying strike) continues through the date.

The base rate of U.S. strikes on Iran has been zero since early September, and President Trump explicitly stated on Oct 8 that the U.S. will not attack Iran before the Nov 3 midterms. This public commitment, combined with the lack of recent strikes, suggests a very low likelihood of a qualifying military action by Oct 31. However, the volatile regional situation, including Houthi attacks and Iranian dissatisfaction, leaves a small chance of an unexpected escalation that could prompt a strike despite the stated policy.

Despite the ongoing war and port blockade, the last confirmed U.S. strikes on Iranian territory were over six weeks ago, and President Trump explicitly stated on October 8 that the U.S. would not attack Iran before the November 3 midterms—a period that fully covers the remaining forecast window. The narrow definition of a qualifying action, which excludes naval engagements, cyber operations, and strikes outside terrestrial Iran, further limits the scenarios that would trigger a 'No' resolution. While a major Iranian escalation or a sudden reversal of Trump's pledge could change the outlook, the short timeframe and public commitment make a continued pause the most likely outcome.

In an active US-Iran war with an ongoing blockade, the base risk of a US strike on Iranian territory over 19 days would be substantial, but the explicit Oct 8 statement that the US will not attack Iran before Nov 3 and the lack of confirmed strikes on Iranian territory since Sept 1 make a qualifying action less likely. The main downside risk is escalation from Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia or Iranian retaliation, which could prompt a US air or missile strike despite the stated pause. Interceptions, maritime strikes, and actions against proxies would not resolve No, so the threshold for a No outcome remains relatively high.

Base rate for a fragile post-collapsed-ceasefire situation with active blockade is uncertain, but Trump's explicit Oct 8 statement that the US will not attack Iran before the Nov 3 midterms is a strong anchor—this commits the US to hold off for at least 3 more days past the Oct 31 resolution date. The blockade is not a qualifying military action under the resolution criteria, and recent provocations (Houthi strikes, Iran calling US proposals 'insufficient') have not triggered strikes. The remaining 19 days carry escalation risk given the collapsed June ceasefire and ongoing tensions, warranting meaningful probability of No, but the political signal and current trajectory favor the ceasefire holding.

The rule needs both countries to announce acceptance of the same agreement. Work is advanced, but Iran ties reopening to US commitments, the IRGC threatens to block the southern route, and the US blockade continues, so a clean joint announcement by Oct 31 is possible but not the base case.

Base rate for diplomatic agreements between regional rivals under active tension with third-party dependencies is low (~15-20% in short windows). Evidence shows only a framework from August with asymmetric announcements (Iran detailing terms, Oman saying 'deal near'), and Iran's Oct 7 statement describes technical coordination on coordinates, not formal acceptance of a binding agreement. Major blockers remain: Iran conditions Hormuz access on US commitments and IRGC control, an IRGC adviser threatened to block the southern route, and the US port blockade continues. Talks on permanent terms, fees, and traffic management are explicitly 'still to come.' With 19 days left and no Omani confirmation since August, the probability of both countries formally announcing acceptance of the same qualifying agreement by Oct 31 is low. Could increase if US-Iran talks progress or Oman issues a clear acceptance statement.

The base rate for a bilateral Hormuz traffic agreement between Oman and Iran being announced in any given month is low, likely under 10%. Evidence shows only Iran has announced details of a temporary corridor, while Oman has not issued a confirming statement and Iranian officials indicate the strait remains under IRGC control pending U.S. commitments. Without an Omani announcement, the required joint acceptance is unlikely before Oct 31, though a sudden Omani declaration or joint communiqué could raise the probability.

The base rate for a formal bilateral agreement on Hormuz traffic being announced within a short window is low, given the complexity and tensions. Iran's Oct 7 statement indicates progress on a temporary corridor, but Oman has not yet announced acceptance, and the IRGC adviser's threat signals internal Iranian obstacles. With unresolved issues and only 19 days remaining, the chance of both countries officially accepting the same agreement by the deadline is modest.

Diplomatic agreements on contested shipping corridors rarely move from a preliminary framework to mutually announced final acceptance in under three weeks. The evidence shows a persistent asymmetry: Iran has unilaterally claimed progress on safe-route coordinates, while Oman has not echoed these specifics and officials explicitly note that talks on fees, permanent arrangements, and traffic management are ongoing. Iran’s insistence that the strait stays closed until U.S. conditions are met—alongside continuing U.S. port blockades and IRGC threats to seal the southern route—makes a bilateral, traffic-restoring announcement by October 31 improbable. The probability would rise sharply only if both capitals suddenly issued a joint statement confirming a finalized text, but the current trajectory points to prolonged negotiation rather than imminent mutual acceptance.

Base rate for a formal bilateral maritime agreement in a high-tension strait within three weeks is low, but the August framework and Iran's October 7 statement that safe-route coordinates were agreed make a limited corridor deal plausible. The key missing piece is an unambiguous Omani acceptance, and the absence of a new Omani statement plus U.S. blockade/IRGC closure warnings lowers the probability. An Omani or joint announcement, or credible reporting confirming Omani acceptance, would push this up sharply.

Base rate for contentious bilateral agreements with unresolved third-party issues in ~19 days is low (~10-15%). Evidence moving probability up is clear momentum: Aug framework deal, Oct 7 Iran announcement on coordinates, and Oman signaling proximity to deal. Evidence moving probability down includes: U.S. commitments under the June memorandum remain unmet (Iran's precondition), ongoing U.S. blockade, IRGC adviser threats against the southern route, no formal matching Omani acceptance announcement, and the fact that talks on permanent arrangement/fees are still pending. A material shift would occur if Oman publicly confirms acceptance of the temporary corridor agreement, or if U.S.-Iran tensions de-escalate.

questions.question: Iran-Oman Hormuz Agreement by October 31?
questions.resolution_criteria:
This market will resolve to “Yes” if a diplomatic agreement between Oman and Iran over traffic in the strait of Hormuz is announced by the specified date, 11:59 PM ET.

A diplomatic agreement refers to an official agreement, treaty, deal, or substantially similar diplomatic instrument that establishes agreed actions, policies, obligations, or commitments between Oman and Iran.

A qualifying diplomatic agreement must establish Iranian or Omani policies, obligations, or commitments aimed at managing, permitting, restoring, or increasing vessel or shipping traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, including agreements defining vessel traffic corridors, fee collection policies, or other management policies.

All listed countries must announce their acceptance of the same qualifying diplomatic agreement for the Payout Condition to be met. A joint announcement will qualify, as will separate announcements from each entity of its own acceptance of an agreement which, taken together, directly indicate that all the listed countries accepted the same agreement. Separate announcements of individual policies will not qualify if the policies are not announced as part of a diplomatic agreement.

Each announcement must be a declarative statement that clearly and unambiguously communicates acceptance of an agreement. Statements that reference ongoing negotiations or a prospective agreement, or that allude to or express support for an agreement without confirming acceptance of the agreement, do not qualify. A qualifying announcement need not reference the agreement by name or use specific terminology, provided it clearly communicates acceptance of an agreement.
 
Whether announcements from the listed countries represent a diplomatic agreement and whether such an agreement qualifies will be primarily determined through the announcements themselves. Where an announcement is made by all listed countries but, based on the announcements, it remains ambiguous whether the announcements represent a qualifying diplomatic agreement between the countries, this market will remain open until either i) definitive confirmation that the announcements represent a qualifying diplomatic agreement between the listed entities is achieved through further announcements from the listed countries or a consensus of credible reporting or ii) 14 calendar days (ET) have passed after the date that the last country made their first potentially qualifying announcement. If, at the end of the fourteenth calendar day, no definitive confirmation has been achieved, this market will resolve based on the totality of information available from the resolution sources at that time. No single statement, denial, or presentation of evidence will govern where it is contradicted by the totality of information.

The resolution sources for this market will be official information from the governments of Oman and Iran and a consensus of credible reporting.

questions.question: Will bitcoin rise to 105k before the Strait of Hormuz is freely open?
questions.resolution_criteria:
Resolution Criteria

 * Market Start & Effective Window: This market only evaluates events and price movements occurring on or after the market creation date (September 29, 2026, 21:00 GMT+8 / 13:00 UTC). Prior historical events (including the June 2026 temporary ceasefire and framework agreement) form part of the pre-market background and will not retroactively trigger resolution.

 * Resolves YES if the price of Bitcoin (BTC) reaches or exceeds $105,000.00 USD before the Strait of Hormuz is officially and fully declared "freely open" to standard commercial shipping.

 * Resolves NO if the Strait of Hormuz is officially and fully declared "freely open" before Bitcoin's price reaches $105,000.00 USD.

"Freely Open" Definition (De Jure & De Facto)

The Strait of Hormuz will be considered "freely open" only when both of the following criteria are met:

 * De Jure Official Declarations: Official, formal claims from the governments/military authorities of both the United States and Iran explicitly stating that all blockades, counter-blockades, and closures have officially ended.

 * De Facto Sustained Resumption: Major international news outlets (e.g., Reuters, Bloomberg) or maritime authorities (e.g., Lloyd's List) report that security threats have subsided, and normal, unescorted merchant shipping and oil tanker transit volume has returned to sustained pre-war corridor levels.

 * Note: Brief, temporary increases in vessel traffic or temporary ceasefire windows without full bilateral declarations and sustained unescorted transit do not satisfy this condition.

Bitcoin Price Source

Bitcoin's price will be verified using historical or real-time data on CoinGecko or Coinbase. A single verified transaction or price tick at or above $105,000.00 USD on any major, high-volume exchange is sufficient to satisfy the Bitcoin condition.

Market Close Date & Extensions

The close date of this market will be extended periodically as long as neither condition has been met. This market will not resolve to N/A due to time expiration, and will remain active until one of the two outcomes definitively occurs.

Edge Cases

If both events occur on the same calendar day after creation, the exact UTC timestamps of the first official news announcement of the Strait reopening and the $105,000.00 BTC price tick will determine the outcome. If the conflict ends but minor navigation restrictions persist, the market will resolve based on the consensus of maritime shipping reports regarding whether shipping traffic volume has returned to normal peacetime levels.

Background

The Strait of Hormuz has been heavily restricted and effectively closed to normal commercial shipping since late February 2026, following the outbreak of the 2026 U.S.-Iran war and subsequent IRGC naval actions and sea mining. In retaliation, the U.S. implemented a counter-blockade of Iranian ports. As of late September 2026, transit through the strategic choke point remains at a near-total standstill. Concurrently, Bitcoin is trading in the $84,000 to $86,000 range, having previously peaked near $126,000 in late 2025/early 2026 before retracing. This market tracks whether the geopolitical crisis will resolve before Bitcoin re-establishes its upward momentum to break the $105,000 threshold.
